html: A cell that has released a cytokine has to be able to hear it again, and the family of receptors on this map is the one that lets it. Each of them is a short device: two chains that hold a kinase apiece before anything binds, a ligand that brings the chains together so the kinases can reach each other, a latent factor in the cytoplasm that the kinases mark on a single tyrosine, and that factor pairing up and crossing into the nucleus. Type I interferon works it one way, with STAT1 and STAT2 marked and joined by IRF9 into the factor that reads the interferon-responsive elements; interleukin-6 and interleukin-10 work it the other, each through a receptor that carries the same kinase and marks the same tyrosine of the same STAT3. That last fact is the uncomfortable one. IL-6 is the cytokine that drives the acute-phase response and IL-10 is the one that shuts inflammation down, and between the receptor and the nucleus they do the same chemistry to the same molecule. The difference is made by a brake and by how long the signal is allowed to run. Both arms induce SOCS3, a small protein whose job is to find a phosphorylated tyrosine on a receptor tail and sit on the kinase next to it. The IL-6 signal transducer has that tyrosine, so IL-6 provokes the protein that silences IL-6, and its signal is a pulse. The IL-10 receptor does not have it, so the same protein, made in the same cell at the same time, leaves the IL-10 signal running, and a sustained STAT3 signal is what an anti-inflammatory programme requires. The proof of how much rests on this is what happens when either half is removed. Take SOCS3 out of a macrophage and IL-6 starts behaving like IL-10, inducing the anti-inflammatory programme it normally never reaches; take STAT3 out of a macrophage and the IL-10 brake disappears, and the animal develops chronic inflammation of the gut. The interferon arm has its own brake in SOCS1, which works further up by binding the activation loop of the kinase itself, and both brakes are made the slow way, as a gene, a transcript and then a protein, which is why the response they control rises before it falls.
